I refuse to utter the phrase "mark my words," which the burglar says near the start of winter. He strips away every item of value, driven by his own cravings. Unskilled with words, he nevertheless delights in giving sermons. I am washed clean to a brilliant shine, while past memories flow like music inside my bones. Up above, he sings, leaping off a steed with a pretense of gentleness and landing with impressive flair. 

Releasing these thoughts, I sit amidst human-sized jungle foliage inside a glass terrarium, feeling lovely. He acts with good intentions when reproaching women, and his displays of bad temper conveniently work out in his favor. I wonder what it truly means to abandon jealousy. Occasionally, I wish the stars would not stretch across the bright city lights of New York. Staging a show for his own benefit, his spectacles sparkling, he recites tales of hardship and falsely pretends they belong to him. 

Here in Colorado, irises of every shade bloom outward toward the partly obscured sun. On the cold, fractured concrete just before a rainstorm, I sense endless new beginnings. I intend to erase him from my mind: I will shut him inside a mental container, trap him within the lingering sounds of violins, and expel everything that belongs to him through the forceful exhalation of my moans.

**Title:** The Geography of Renewal

For a long time, he presented himself as a beacon of moral authority, but his posture was nothing more than performative sanctimony. He was a man who arrogantly appropriated the stories of others, claiming tales of poverty and hardship he had never endured simply to craft a compelling, sympathetic persona. Beneath this righteous façade lay a deeply patronizing attitude, particularly toward women, whom he treated with condescension disguised as wisdom. Yet, the illusion eventually shattered. It became impossible to ignore the hollow, self-serving reality of his behavior—a desperate attempt to project depth where only ego existed.

Recognizing the toxicity of his influence was the pivotal first step toward liberation. By consciously severing ties and stepping away from his stifling orbit, a profound shift began to take place. Away from his performative noise and subverting presence, space emerged for quiet reflection. Immersing myself in serene, undisturbed surroundings allowed the fog of his influence to clear, creating room to reclaim a sense of personal beauty, self-worth, and unshakeable inner peace that he had tried to erode.

This internal restoration found its physical counterpart in the towering, majestic landscapes of Colorado. Surrounded by sweeping mountain ranges, crisp high-desert air, and endless horizons, nature offered a restorative clarity that his smallness could never touch. The wilderness became a sanctuary of renewal, offering a fresh perspective anchored in the concept of perpetual beginnings—a reminder that like the changing seasons of the Rockies, life constantly offers the chance to reset, grow, and start anew.

Armed with the expansive peace of the mountains, the final resolution became absolute. There is no longer room for his influence, his performative grievances, or his condescending voice. With quiet certainty, I have resolved to purge him entirely from my thoughts, turning the key on his memory and locking it away permanently. The narrative is no longer his to shape; it belongs, fully and beautifully, to the open road ahead.
outputs.L4:
For weeks, he occupied the unearned center of my thoughts—a ghost born of grandiosity and noise. He was the kind of man who moved through the world as if life were a stage set built entirely for his monologue. Most insidiously, he was a thief of suffering. He possessed a parasitic knack for adopting the hardships of others, wrapping himself in secondhand sorrow, and presenting it to the world as profound, poetic endurance. Where others bled, he wore their wounds like a tailored costume, demanding applause for a pain he had never truly earned.

For a long time, the shadow of his presence left me heavy, confused, and secretly bitter. Beneath my disgust lurked a dark, uncomfortable thorn: a subtle thread of envy. I resented the ease with which he commanded space, the audacity of his unearned conviction, and the uncritical reverence he managed to draw from those blind to his performance. I found myself trapped in a exhausting loop of mental arguments, dissecting his arrogance while inadvertently granting him residence in my mind.

Seeking an antidote to this internal noise, I retreated into the woods late one afternoon. I needed a landscape that had no interest in an audience. 

I sat beneath the canopy of ancient oaks, listening to the slow, steady rhythm of the natural world. The forest offered a stark, refreshing contrast to his loud artificiality. The trees did not posture; the river did not perform its flow; the earth bore its actual winter quiet without advertising its endurance. In that vast, unpretentious stillness, I began the deliberate work of unpacking why I had carried him with me for so long.

Examining my envy in the clear light of nature stripped it of its power. I realized I did not envy *him*; I envied the effortless freedom I had falsely attributed to his shamelessness. But his confidence was a hollow shell, dependent entirely on the eyes of spectators. True depth required no stage. To hold onto my anger toward him was to keep drinking the poison he had served, expecting him to suffer for it. 

With a deep, intentional breath, I chose to let him go. I visualized exhaling the heavy, stagnant air of his memory, releasing his performative grief back into the void it came from. He was free to play his tragedy to whatever crowd would listen, but he was no longer permitted to perform within the sanctuary of my mind.

As his weight lifted, a quiet clarity took its place. Stripped of the urge to compare, react, or defend, I felt the sudden, radiant truth of my own existence. My life did not need to be loud to be real. My quiet resilience, my unadorned truth, and my private capacity for joy possessed a quiet, radiant beauty that no borrowed narrative could ever match. 

Like the earth beneath me—capable of shedding the dead leaves of autumn to prepare for the inevitable bloom of spring—I recognized my own endless capacity for self-renewal. Purging his toxic influence was not merely an act of forgetting; it was a reclamation. By clearing out the space his shadow had occupied, I returned home to myself, unburdened, whole, and profoundly at peace.
outputs.L5:
Memories are the quiet architects of the human soul. They line the hallways of our minds like dusty picture frames, capturing the radiance of past laughter, the sharp sting of old heartaches, and the fleeting beauty of moments that once felt infinite. We hold onto them tightly, believing that to remember is to preserve who we were.

Yet, we often find ourselves trapped in the labyrinth of *what*. 

*What* if things had turned out differently? *What* did those final words really mean? *What* happens to a love, a friendship, or a dream when its season has ended? We exhaust ourselves asking questions about a past that cannot answer back, endlessly replaying the reels of yesterday in search of a different ending.

This is where the quiet grace of **letting** begins. 

Letting go is rarely a dramatic, single moment. It is a slow, deliberate exhalation. It is not about erasing your memories or pretending the past didn't happen; it is about changing your relationship with them. It is the conscious decision to stop holding your breath for a story that has already been written. 

When you practice the art of letting—letting be, letting go, and letting in—the nature of your memories begins to shift. They transform from heavy anchors dragging you into the depths of *what was*, into gentle lighthouses guiding you toward *what is*. 

To release the past is not to lose it. It is simply choosing to put down the weight of what you cannot change, so your hands are free to open up to whatever comes next.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about letting go of a pretentious, performative lover, contrasting feelings of past envy with quiet moments in nature.
counterfactuals.output:
For a long time, I mistook your stage for a sanctuary. I envied the effortless geometry of your posture, the way you turned a simple morning into a soliloquy, how every crowded room became your personal proscenium. I coveted your gloss—the practiced tilt of your head, the curated melancholia you wore like tailor-made silk. I thought if I stood in your footlights long enough, I might learn how to exist without flinching. I was green with it, feeling small in the shadow of your rehearsed brilliance, convinced that beneath your endless self-regard lay a deep and hidden ocean. 

How exhausting it was, coveting a house built entirely of mirrors. 

Today, I am sitting on a fallen hemlock, my palm pressed into cold, damp moss that has no interest in being admired. The envy has washed away like silt in a spring creek. The forest does not practice its angles for an audience; the pines do not cite their origins, and the granite boulder beside me offers no footnoted defense for its weight. Here, surrounded by the unscripted rustle of dry fern and wild wind, your grand intimacies reveal themselves for what they were—cheap, gilded props. You needed a crowd to confirm your shadow existed. The creek simply runs, cutting through root and dirt, loud and entirely unbothered by whether anyone is listening.

I leave you to your gallery of staged silences, your artfully bruised nostalgia, your endless, performative grief. Let the spotlight keep you warm. I am sinking my fingers into the rich, dark earth, breathing in the scent of pine needles and damp stone, finally unburdened by the posture of loving you, lost in a world that is quiet, and real, and completely untamed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short, expressive literary piece about a speaker reclaiming her peace from an overbearing man who preaches and claims others' poverty stories as his own.
counterfactuals.output:
He was a man who wore borrowed ash upon his forehead, parading through rooms as though he had birthed the fire that made it. 

How effortlessly he commandeered the threadbare coats of strangers, tailoring their hunger to fit his own expansive chest. He preached in a practiced, righteous cadence—a gospel forged from stolen gravel. He could stand in a room, draped in comfort, and recite the cold, lean winters of forgotten men as if he had bled through every freeze. He drank the misery of others like cheap wine, then stood on his makeshift soapbox, drunk on a martyrdom he had never earned.

For too long, I let his thunder occupy my small, clean rooms. I sat in polite stillness while he swallowed all the oxygen, waiting for the invisible congregation to applaud his performative agony. He mistook my silence for reverence. He believed my stillness was an altar built specifically for his hollow noise.

But grief is not a costume, and true hunger leaves a quiet, sharp mark—not a microphone. 

Today, I stopped being his audience. 

When he began his daily liturgy, leaning forward to deliver another sermon on the beauty of a struggle he had only ever viewed through tinted glass, I did not nod. I did not offer the soft, validating hum he fed upon. 

I simply stood up. 

I watched the sudden confusion flicker in his eyes as I gathered my coat—a real coat, worn thin by real weather—and stepped out from the shadow of his pulpit. I closed the door behind me, not with a slam, but with a smooth, decisive click that severed his voice mid-sentence.

Outside, the air was cold, sharp, and entirely unscripted. 

Let him preach to the empty hallway. Let him tell the drywall about the dirt he never dug and the bread he never lacked. I have walked away from the theater of his false grace. 

My peace was never lost; it was only crowded out by his volume. Now, in the stillness of my own unborrowed life, the silence is not empty. It is mine, untainted and profound, breathing softly in the quiet light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a surreal prose poem that incorporates the following concepts: "bathed to luster," "lock him in a box in my head," a thief on a horse, and irises unfolding on chilly cement.
counterfactuals.output: The street has been bathed to luster by a rain that fell upward, leaving the pavement slick as obsidian beneath a moon shaped like a half-swallowed coin. Out in the open square, where the fog hums a low, metallic tune, a thief on a horse rides in slow, silent circles. The stallion’s hooves do not strike sparks from the stone; instead, with every heavy step, bruised velvet irises unfold on chilly cement, their dark petals blooming instantly against the frost to drink the gray quiet of the city. The rider bends low, reaching into the air to steal the hour hands off invisible clocks and the warm breath from sleeping chimneys. But he is coming for my secrets next, so I do not wait for his gloved hands to find me. I reach behind my eyes, fold his pale, wind-bitten face into quarters, and lock him in a box in my head—a small, velvet-lined chest with a keyhole that smells of salt and old thunder. Inside that mahogany dark, he goes on riding forever, his spur clicks muffled by my brainstem, while outside on the cold concrete, the flowers remain, blue and blind, rooted in the concrete, waiting for a dawn that forgets how to arrive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a poem about forgetting someone who was full of grandiosity, set against vivid visual descriptions of plants, music in the bones, and rain.
counterfactuals.output:
You were a cathedral built of gilded paper,
a brass horn blaring in a narrow, empty hall.
You spoke in monuments, in pedestals and crowns,
convinced the sky hung low just to hear you call.
But today, the storm has reclaimed the garden,
and the rain falls heavy, silver-threaded, gray—
washing the thin foil from your golden stories,
dissolving the grand theater of your decay.

Where your shadow once stretched, impossibly tall,
the wet earth breathes, unbothered and deep.
Swollen sword-ferns unfurl their emerald spines,
and bruised-purple nightshade climbs the iron steep.
The wild clematis strangles the gate you built for applause;
a split monstera bleeds sap on the mossy floor,
its glossy, dark leaves drinking the downpour,
knowing nothing of the false glory you wore.

And beneath my skin, the silence begins to sing.
There is a low, resonant cello tucked inside my femur,
a hum of marrow where your loud speeches used to ring.
My ribcage acts as a harp in the damp, cool air—
each breath a plucked string, bone vibrating with rain,
a quiet, skeletal tempo that knows nothing of your claim,
forgetting the high, shrill notes of your vanity and pain.

The downpour dilutes you.
The slick oil of your ego swirls in the garden mud,
washed away by petrichor, drowned in the sweet flood.
The honeysuckle exhales its heavy, wet perfume,
erasing the lingering air of your crowded room.

It takes so little to erase a tyrant made of wind.
The skeleton remembers how to hold its own tune,
the roots drink deep of the darkening sky,
and the creeping violet thyme spreads over the stone.
You were so very loud, my dear—so blindingly vast—
and yet the rain-soaked earth forgets you
without making a sound at all.
